notes.meaning: Moab is told to send a tribute of lambs to the king in Jerusalem. A tribute is a payment a weaker nation makes to a stronger king. Moab's king once paid Israel in lambs but stopped after Ahab died (2 Kings 3:4-5). Now Moab is urged to pay Judah instead, which means submitting to David's royal family as its only safety. Matthew Henry also applies this to us: come to God, the great Ruler, in the name of the Lamb of God, and give yourselves to him.

differ.view: Some Reformed teachers read the lamb as a sacrifice for God's temple on Mount Zion. They take the command as mockery: Moab would gladly make peace now, but its repentance comes too late.

notes.meaning: Moab's people are pictured as young birds pushed out of the nest. They flutter about, scared and unsure where to go. "Daughters of Moab" means the people of Moab, or its women. They gather at the river Arnon, Moab's border, trying to cross and escape. Matthew Henry warns that those who will not shelter under God end up afraid of everything else.

Here Moab's refugees plead with Zion, the people of Judah. They ask for advice and a decision about their fate. They want shelter as thick as night's darkness under the blazing noon sun, so their enemies cannot see them. They beg Judah not to hand over those fleeing to the people chasing them.

The plea goes on: let Moab's fugitives stay in Judah and be safe from the destroyer. Then comes the reason Moab can trust Judah. The oppressor, probably Assyria, will soon be gone. The destruction will stop, and the trampling armies will vanish from the land.

differ.view: Many older Protestant commentators read "my outcasts" as God's own people, Israel. God still owns them while he disciplines them. On this reading God tells Moab to hide them, and anyone who hopes for kindness in trouble should show kindness to refugees.

notes.meaning: After the oppressor is gone, God will set up a throne in David's family out of his own loving kindness. A faithful king will sit on it. He will search out what is right and be quick to do justice, never delaying it. Hezekiah was a partial picture of this king, but the promise points most fully to Christ and his lasting kingdom.

differ.view: Some read verses 4-5 as end-times prophecy. Jewish people flee the Antichrist and find shelter, and then the Messiah sets up his throne and reigns.

notes.meaning: Moab was well known for its pride. It was puffed up, conceited, and quick to anger. That pride kept Moab from taking the good advice to submit. Its proud boasts are empty and will not come true. Matthew Henry notes that pride ruins more people than almost any other sin.

Because of its pride, the whole nation will wail together over its ruin. Kir-hareseth was Moab's chief fortress city. Its raisin cakes, made from the fine grapes of the region, are now gone, and the people mourn them. Some older translations read "foundations," picturing the city torn down to its base.

Moab was famous for its fields and vineyards. The vines of Sibmah had spread north to Jazer, out into the desert, and down to the Dead Sea. Now invading rulers, the Assyrians and other enemies, have trampled the best vines. The whole fruitful land is laid waste.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many later scholars read it the other way round: Sibmah's wine was so strong it "struck down," or made drunk, the rulers of the nations. This would praise the wine's fame before its loss.

notes.meaning: The prophet weeps for Moab, even though it is a foreign and hostile nation. He soaks Heshbon and Elealeh with his tears. The happy shouts of harvest are gone. Many say the enemy's battle cry has fallen on the harvest instead. Matthew Henry notes that Jesus, the great prophet, also knew grief like this.

All joy is gone from the orchards and vineyards. No one sings while treading grapes in the winepress. Then God himself speaks: "I have put an end to the cheering." Human armies do the damage, but it is God's just punishment. Matthew Henry notes that joy in God is better than harvest joy, because no one can take it away.

The prophet's heart aches for Moab. His deep inner feelings tremble like harp strings being played. The Bible often speaks of the inner parts of the body as the place of deep pity. God's people should feel sorrow even for the troubles of the wider world.

Moab wears itself out praying at its high places, the hilltop shrines for idols. Then it goes to its main temple, likely that of its god Chemosh, to pray. None of it will help. Like the prophets of Baal in Elijah's day, Moab prays to a god who cannot hear or save.
All of this is a message the Lord had given about Moab earlier. It came from God, not from the prophet. Because God has spoken it, nothing can stop it from happening.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many scholars think Isaiah is repeating an oracle first given by an earlier prophet, and adding a new time limit.

notes.meaning: Now God sets a date: within three years. A hired worker counts his contract years exactly, so these three years are exact too. Moab's glory, wealth and large population will become a thing of scorn. Only a small, weak group will be left. Wesley sees this as a heavy Assyrian blow, with Moab's final ruin coming later under Nebuchadnezzar. Matthew Henry notes that this fair warning also gave Moab time to repent.
